title: Cu/Cu2O Electrodes and CO2 Reduction to Formic Acid: Effects of Organic Additives on Surface Morphology and Activity
abstract: Copper/copper oxide (Cu/Cu2O) electrodes are known to display interesting electrocatalytic performances for the reduction of CO2, and thus, deserve further investigation for optimization. Here, we show that the addition of nitrogen-based organic additives greatly improves the activity of these electrodes (higher current densities, greater selectivity, and higher faradaic yields). The best effector is found to be tetramethyl cyclam. For example, electrolysis at 2.0 V versus Fc/Fc in CO2-saturated DMF/H2O (99:1, v/v) in the presence of this effector results in formic acid with almost 90 % faradaic yield. SEM and XPS analysis of the electrode surface reveals that the organic additive promotes the formation of active Cu nanoparticles from Cu2O during electrolysis. This simple approach provides a straightforward strategy toward the optimization of Cu/Cu2O electrodes.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Since Hori’s seminal work 30 years ago, it has been known that only a few transition metal catalysts show pronounced catalytic activities for CO2 electroreduction.
[1–3] Among them, polycrystalline copper has become an attractive option because of its ability to reduce CO2 by multiple electrons generating not only formic acid and carbon monoxide but also methanol, methane, and ethylene, albeit at very negative redox potentials.[4–7]
Based on a relatively cheap and abundant non-noble metal, copper electrodes constitute an exciting candidate for the development of CO2 electrolyzers, and thus, deserve much more effort to improve their performances. For example, very recently, Cu0 particles, with an optimized surface area derived from the electroreduction of Cu2O layers, were shown to display increased activity, better selectivity for CO2 reduction with regard to proton reduction, and greater stability.[8–11] In particular, these electrodes could catalyze the electroreduction of CO2 to formic acid and carbon monoxide in bicarbonate electrolyte with high faradaic yields at low overpotentials.[8] An original active and stable electrocatalytic copper-based material for the selective reduction of CO2 to formic acid in DMF/H2O solutions has been obtained through electrodeposition starting from a homogeneous cyclam (cyclam = 1,4,8,11-tetraazacycloteradecane, 1) complex of copper.[12] Note that tin-based electrodes
are also good catalytic materials for CO2 conversion to formic acid.[13] Furthermore, several reports have shown important effects of surface pretreatment and nanostructuration of Cubased electrodes on their catalytic performances (selectivity, overpotentials, stability, formation of multicarbon products) toward CO2 electroreduction. [14, 15]
We now report on the discovery that CO2 electroreduction using standard Cu/Cu2O-modified FTO electrodes is greatly

The simplicity of the method for the preparation of active Cu-based electrodes is remarkable. Screening organic compounds as effectors of CO2 electroreduction activity with the aim of optimizing the system thus becomes practically facile. Within the chosen set of substrates, tetramethyl cyclam (3) was found to give the best performances. Detailed physicochemical analysis of the material surface strongly suggests that the additive stimulates the quick formation and the stabilization of catalytically active Cu0 nanoparticles.

sections.heading: Chemicals
sections.text: All chemicals including cyclam (1, 98 %), 1,8-dimethyl cyclam (2), 1,4,8,11-tetramethyl cyclam (3), 1,4,7-triazacyclononane (4), diethylenetriamine (5), 18-crown-6 (6), tetrabutylammonium tetrafluoroborate (nBu4NBF4, 99 %), Cu(ClO4)2·6 H2O (99.9 %), CuSO4·5 H2O, lactic acid (85 % in water), DMF (99.8 %), and MeCN (99.9 %) were purchased from Sigma–Aldrich. Fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO, 600 nm) coated glass slides with 7 W/sq surface resistivity were purchased from Solems (France). They were rinsed with acetone and deionized water in a sonication bath prior to use. Cu2O films were deposited by electrodeposition from 0.2 m CuSO4·5 H2O and 3 m lactic acid in 0.5 m K2HPO4/K3PO4 aqueous buffer (pH 12) at a constant current of 0.1 mA cm 2 and 1 C charge passed per cm2.[16]

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text:
SEM images and energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) spectra were recorded with an FEG-SEM (Zeiss- Leo 1530) operating at 10 kV and equipped with a Bruker SDD EDX detector.
The X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analyses were performed with a F PHYSICAL ELECTRONICS versaProbe II spectrometer under microfocused (diameter of irradiated area = 200 mm) monochromatized AlKa radiation (1486.6 eV). The residual pressure inside the analysis chamber was 7 10 8 Pa. A fixed analyzer pass energy of 23 eV was used for core level scans, leading to an overall energy resolution of 0.6 eV. Survey spectra were captured at a pass energy of 117 eV. The photoelectron takeoff angle was 458, which provided an integrated sampling depth of approximately 5 nm. All samples were analyzed under a dual argon ion (5 eV) and electron (4 eV) beam charge neutralization allowing simultaneous, positive and negative, charge neutralization without chemical state modification. All spectra were referenced against an internal signal, typically by adjusting the C 1s level peak at a binding energy of 284.8 eV. Analysis performed without charge neutralization shows a shift of 6 eV to higher binding energies of all peaks in the raw spectra, but results in similar spectra without any change in the chemical signatures after calibration of the C 1s level peak at a binding energy of 284.8 eV.
The X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) patterns were recorded using an X’Pert Pro P analytical diffractometer equipped with either a CuKa radiation source (lKa1 = 1.540598 , lKa2 = 1.544426 ) or a CoKa radiation source (lKa1 = 1.78897 , lKa2 = 1.79285 ) with an X’Celerator detector. Rietveld refinements[23] were performed with the Full Prof suite of programs.
Electrochemical measurements were performed in a three-electrode, two-compartment cell using a Bio-logic SP300 potentiostat.
FTO-coated glass electrodes, rinsed with acetone and deionized water, were used as working electrodes throughout the study. Electrolytic tape (Radiospare: ref. 468–421) was used to define a 1 cm2 electrode surface area. The FTO electrode was connected to the potentiostat with an alligator clip. A Ag/AgCl/3 m KCl (hereafter abbreviated Ag/AgCl) reference electrode was placed in the same compartment as the working electrode. The XPS survey confirmed that no silver was deposited onto the electrode surface after electrochemical measurements. A platinum counter electrode was placed in a separate compartment connected by a glass frit and filled with the same electrolytic solution. All potential values are reported versus the potential of the Fc+/Fc couple added as an internal standard to the solution after the measurements.
Hydrogen evolution was analyzed with a PerkinElmer Clarus 500 gas chromatography instrument equipped with a porapack Q 80/ 100 column (6’ 1/8“) thermostated at 40 8C and a TCD detector thermostated at 100 8C. Carbon monoxide was detected with a gas chromatograph (Shimadzu GC-2010) equipped with a methanizer, a flame induction detector (FID), and a shincarbon ST (Restek) column. Formate concentrations were determined by ionic exchange chromatography (883 Basic IC, Metrohm). Formaldehyde was analyzed using NASH's reagent and chromotropic acid methods.[17, 18]
Analysis of the Cu-based modified electrode after electrolysis in the presence of teramethyl cyclam) was performed as follows. The electrode was removed from the electrolytic cell and washed several times with the same solution of aqueous hydrochloric acid (100 mL of 6 m HCl). The aliquots were collected together, and neutralized by adding Na2CO3 (4.9 mL, 60 mm). After evaporation to dryness, water (500 mL) and an excess of CuCl2·2 H2O (1 mg) were added. After 10 min, the suspension was centrifuged and the supernatant was analyzed by reverse phase HPLC on an Xbridge C18 column (Waters). Tetramethyl cyclam detection was achieved by UV absorbance at 260 nm using a calibration curve obtained from tetramethyl cyclam solutions treated similarly. 13C-formic acid analysis was performed by 13C NMR spectroscopy. A Cu2O electrode was used for electrolysis in DMF/3 % H2O (containing 1 mm 3) under 13CO2 saturation. A constant potential of 2.0 V versus Fc+/Fc was applied for the reduction of 13CO2. After 3 h, a 13C-formic acid concentration of 3.8 mm was determined by ionic exchange chromatography. For 13C NMR characterization, CD3CN (0.2 mL) was added to the electrolysis solution (0.8 mL).

sections.heading: CO2 electroreduction on Cu/Cu2O electrodes
sections.text:
According to previously reported procedures, Cu2O films were deposited on FTO electrodes by electroreduction of pH 12 aqueous solutions of copper sulfate in the presence of lactate.[16] Under standard conditions, electrodeposition is carried out at a constant potential of 0.3 V versus Ag/AgCl for a total passed charge of 1 C cm 2. As shown in Figure 1, this electrode allows electroreduction of CO2 in CO2-saturated DMF/H2O (97:3, v/v) solutions in the presence of tetrabutylammonium tetrafluoroborate (nBu4NBF4) salt as the electrolyte, at an applied potential of 2.0 V versus Fc+/Fc, albeit with a low current density (0.4 mA cm 2). The electrocatalytic activity is probably caused by the formation of active Cu0 species.[8] We hereafter designate this material as the Cu/Cu2O electrode. After 1 h electrolysis, the charge passed was 1.6 C; the reaction

Stimulation of CO2 electroreduction on Cu/Cu2O electrodes by cyclam
As shown in Figure 1, the addition of 1 mm cyclam during the course of the electrolysis resulted in a drastic change in the activity of the Cu/Cu2O electrode. The current density increased rapidly from 0.4 mA cm 2 and reached a stable value of 1.2 mA cm 2. The current density increased as a function of cyclam concentration up to 1 mm. Larger concentrations had no further effect on the activity. The same current density was obtained when cyclam was added in the initial electrolyte before the start of the electrolysis (Figure 1, blue trace). After 1 h, the charge passed was 4.3 C, and the products were formate (51 %), H2 (41 %), and CO (3 %), with a total faradaic yield of 95 %.
Screening organic compounds for stimulation of CO2 electroreduction on Cu/Cu2O electrodes
The effect of cyclam reported above affords a simple protocol to study the effect of various compounds on the performances of Cu/Cu2O electrodes. Screening a library of compounds can thus be done very simply by adding 1 mm of a given compound to a standard electrolytic solution and running controlled-potential electroreduction of CO2 for one hour. Each compound is thus characterized by the following parameters : i) current density; ii) charge passed as a function of time; iii) Faradaic yield for each reaction product. We present in Table 1 and Figure 2 the results obtained with a set of N- and O-based organic compounds (Scheme 1). Considering the large stimulating effect of cyclam (1) we studied structural analogues, namely, 1,8-dimethyl cyclam (2), 1,4,8,11-tetramethyl cyclam (3), 1,4,7-triazacyclononane (4), and diethylenetriamine (5). 18-C-6 crown ether (6) was used to compare N-based additives with O-based ones. The data clearly show that the performances of the Cu/Cu2O electrodes depend greatly on the structure of the organic additive. Electrolytic current density values range from 0.7 to 1.5 mA cm 2 in the order 6<5<4< 1<2<3. In all cases, the currents were larger than those obtained in the absence of any additive. The best effector was compound 3, which was shown to be present at the surface of the electrode with a surface concentration of 10 2 nmol cm 2

In all cases, CO was a very minor product (1–4 %), and total faradaic yields were above 90 %. In the case of compound 3, the same controlled potential electrolytic experiment was performed, under identical conditions, but using a solution saturated with 13CO2 as the substrate. After 3 h reaction, 3.8 mm formic acid was produced. Analysis of that product by NMR showed that only 13C-labeled formic acid was detected (Figure S1, Supporting Information).

sections.heading: Optimization of electrocatalytic performances
sections.text:
The effect of the applied potential during electrolysis was also studied (Figure S2 and Table S1, Supporting Information). Shifting the applied potential to more negative values resulted in a drastic increase in the electrolytic current, but also led to a significant increase in the H2/formate ratio. Higher faradaic yields of CO were obtained at more negative potentials.
The large production of hydrogen in these systems led us to study the effect of water on the selectivity of the reaction. The data shown in Table 2 (and Figure S3, Supporting Information,
in the case of compound 3) demonstrate that stable current densities were obtained during electroreduction of CO2 in DMF/H2O (99:1, v/v) with cumulative faradaic yields above 90 %. Remarkably, faradaic yields for formate greatly increased, reaching 86 % in the case of compound 3, and thus, making the system highly selective for the conversion of CO2 to formic acid. Note that, on the basis of charge values and faradaic yields, the total amount of formate produced after 1 h reaction was the same whether the solution contained 3 % or 1 % water. Thus, water content essentially affected hydrogen formation. Under these optimized conditions, a long-term electrolysis was performed. The current density remained stable during the 3 h experiment (Figure S4, Supporting Information).
Figure 3 shows the polarization curves of a Cu/Cu2O electrode measured in the absence and presence of the best effector (compound 3) in CO2-saturated DMF/H2O (99:1, v/v), for which catalysis predominantly produces formate. Both curves display a similar onset potential for electrocatalytic current at 1.6 V versus Fc+/Fc, corresponding to a moderate overpotential of 250 mV.[12] A Tafel slope of approximately 120 mV dec 1
was derived from the data of Figure 3. Such a value has often been reported in the case of systems (metallic electrodes) for which the one-electron reduction of CO2 to CO2C
is the ratelimiting step.[2]
Characterization of the modified Cu/Cu2O electrodes
The Cu/Cu2O electrodes obtained in the absence of any additive and in the presence of either 3 or 5, the additives responsible for high and low catalytic activity enhancement, respectively, were characterized by a variety of methods.
SEM images clearly show that the surface of a Cu/Cu2O electrode (compare Figure 4 A and B) is modified only very slightly during electrolysis in the absence of any additive. In contrast, the presence of 3 promoted a significant modification of the electrode surface. Three minutes after addition of 3 to the electrolytic solution, the surface of the electrode was already modified (Figure 4 D), and appeared different from those seen in Figure 4 A and B. The coating became more compact and uniform after 1 h electrolysis (Figure 4 E; Cu NPs are then 200 nm in diameter). Remarkably, the surface of the electrode was essentially unaffected after 1 h electrolysis in the presence of a weak effector such as compound 5 (Figure 4 C). EDX spectroscopy (Figure 4 F) showed a net increase in the Cu/ O ratio during electrolysis, in line with the conversion of Cu2O into Cu NPs during electrolysis.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text:
Copper is one of the most attractive metals for CO2 electrocatalytic reduction, and therefore, has been under scrutiny for years. However, before developing marketable technological devices based on Cu electrodes, a number of limitations (stability, overpotentials, selectivity, and so on) need to be overcome. Recent studies have shown that the performances of Cu electrodes are strongly affected by their pretreatment and by modification of their surface structures. More specifically, the formation of Cu0 nanoparticles seems to be critical for greater efficiency and selectivity.[8–10, 14, 15] Starting from standard Cu2O films electrodeposited on an FTO electrode, with low activity, we have discovered that the formation of active and stable Cu0 nanoparticles at the surface of the Cu2O electrode can be stimulated greatly by the simple addition of tetramethyl cyclam (compound 3) during electrolysis. Compound 3 was selected on the basis of comparisons with other N- and O-based organic compounds. This study indeed revealed a clear effect of the structure of the organic additive on the activity of the Cu/Cu2O electrode. This electrode, treated with 3, can thus achieve electroreduction of CO2 with high selectivity toward the formation of formic acid, with a small amount of CO, in DMF/water solutions. H2 is also produced, but with yields controlled by the amount of water in the electrolyte. For example, electrolysis at 2.0 V versus Fc+/Fc in CO2-saturated DMF/H2O (99:1, v/v) resulted in formic acid with almost 90 % faradaic yield. Under these conditions, a current density up to 1 mA cm 2 can be obtained at an overpotential of 710 mV. Such a value compares well with those measured for recently described Cu,[12] Mo,[21] and Bi-based[22, 23] materials for the selective reduction of CO2 in DMF or acetonitrile.
Detailed analysis of the material surface provided some insight into the function of the organic additive. SEM and XPS analyses clearly revealed that the organic additives promote, to various extents, the formation and stabilization of Cu0 nanoparticles from Cu2O during electrolysis at low potentials. These Cu NPs act as the active catalytic species for CO2 reduction and formic acid production.[8] Correlation of XPS, XRD, and EDX data with electrocatalytic measurements clearly demonstrates that the higher the amount of Cu0 at the surface of the electrode, the higher the current density for CO2 reduction. It is therefore likely that the additive, which is retained in the final material, participates in the structuration of the surface during accumulation of Cu0 NPs, essential for activity, and possibly also in the stabilization of such a morphology, in line with the observed stabilization of the electrolytic current densities.
It is clear that multi-N atoms are superior to multi-O atoms within the additive structure. Furthermore, a cyclic structure appears to be more efficient than its linear analogue. This is reminiscent of such compounds acting as ligands of copper ions. However, cyclam (1) is a much better ligand for CuII ions than the best tetramethyl cyclam (3), with a log K value of 27.2 (as compared to 18.3 for compound 3).[24] Interestingly, recent studies have shown that amines behave as ligands binding at Cu0 surfaces.[25, 26] It is thus possible that compound 3 promotes the formation of Cu0 NPs and stabilizes them through such in-
teractions. Whether, in addition, it favors CO2 capture at the surface of the electrode or stabilizes catalytically competent reaction intermediates or activates the Cu NPs through transient formation of 3-CuNP assemblies is an exciting but challenging hypothesis that remains to be studied. During the course of this investigation, several studies consistently reported stimulating effects of N-based compounds on the CO2 reduction electrocatalytic activities of metallic surfaces. Gewirth and collaborators observed that the addition of diaminotriazole to a Ag electrode resulted in a CO2 reduction activity with slightly lower overpotential.[27] MacFarlane and co-workers described polyethylenimine-promoted electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to CO by graphene-supported amorphous molybdenum sulfide.[28] Finally, amino acids, especially glycine, were shown to drive Cu-based electrodes toward hydrocarbon formation.[29] In that case, calculations suggested that this could be caused by the stabilization of key intermediates by adsorbed glycine.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: The combination of inorganic materials and organic effectors, such as the one described in this study, in the context of multielectron catalysis is a new field that has been explored very little. Here, we have shown that this approach is a simple and practical strategy for the development of new Cu-based materials for new energy-storage technologies. Further extensive screening should be undertaken to better identify the structure–activity relationships and allow the production of even more efficient ligand-promoted Cu/Cu2O electrodes. There are many ways by which N-based compounds might modulate the activity of metallic electrodes for CO2 reduction, briefly discussed above. This is also an exciting issue that has not yet been addressed.

sections.heading: Cu/Cu2O Electrodes and CO2 Reduction to Formic Acid: Effects of Organic Additives on Surface
sections.text:
Morphology and Activity
Additives for activity : Nitrogen-based organic additives greatly improve the activity of Cu/Cu2O electrodes for the electroreduction of CO2, which exhibit higher current densities, greater selectivity, and higher faradaic yields (see figure). It is shown that they promote
the formation of active Cu0 nanoparticles from Cu2O during electrolysis. This simple approach provides a straightforward strategy toward the optimization of Cu/Cu2O electrodes for the electroreduction of CO2.
